titles.text: Simeon b. Shetah President of the Court

description.en: During the tumultuous reign of Alexander Yannai, the third pair of the Zugot, Yehudah ben Tabbai and Shimon ben Shetach, faced significant challenges. Despite being Yannai's brother-in-law, Shimon had to go into hiding during Yannai's persecution of the Pharisees, while Yehudah fled to Egypt. Nonetheless, Shimon successfully wrested control of the Sanhedrin from the Sadducees.
description.he: הזוג השלישי, יהודה בן טבאי ושמעון בן שטח, כיהנו בתקופה הסוערת של שלטון אלכסנדר ינאי. אף ששמעון היה גיסו של ינאי, הוא נאלץ להסתתר בשיאה של רדיפת הפרושים על ידי ינאי, ויהודה ברח למצרים. למרות זאת הצליח שמעון להשיג שליטה על הסנהדרין במקום הצדוקים.

en.prompt: The Gemara debate in Chagigah 16b delves into the roles of Nasi and deputy Nasi in halakhic rulings. It questions whether a deputy Nasi, like Shimon ben Shetach, can issue rulings in the presence of the Nasi, focusing on the protocols and authority dynamics within the Beit Din (Jewish court).
en.ai_prompt: The debate between two prominent sages highlights the complexities of halakhic authority and the roles of Nasi and deputy Nasi. The Gemara discusses whether a deputy Nasi can issue halakhic rulings in the presence of the Nasi, focusing on the commitment made by one sage to rule only in the presence of the other.

en.title: The Influence of Shelomith
en.prompt: Shimon ben Shetach's return to Jerusalem and the Sanhedrin was aided by familial support and strategic political moves. Pirkei Avot, a tractate of the Mishnah, includes teachings from Shimon ben Shetach, who lived during the reign of Alexander Janneus and Shelomith, his sister. Despite persecution, he escaped, returned to Jerusalem with his sister's assistance, and reclaimed his role in the Sanhedrin from Sadducee influence.
en.ai_prompt: The return to Jerusalem and the Sanhedrin was significantly influenced by familial support and political maneuvering. Pirkei Avot, a tractate of the Mishnah, offers ethical teachings and maxims from the Rabbis, traditionally studied on Shabbat afternoons between Passover and Rosh Hashanah.

en.title: Ethical Judging
en.prompt: Judah ben Tabbai and Shimon ben Shetach, pivotal figures in Jewish tradition, imparted timeless wisdom on judicial ethics. Judah ben Tabbai advised judges to maintain impartiality, cautioning against advocacy for either party. He taught to initially view litigants as potentially guilty, yet to consider them innocent once judgment was accepted.
